title: 无需 A/B 测试，如何把 AI 安全交付给百万患者｜Jared Joselowitz 与 Ufonia
author: AI Engineer
content:
Brief Description

Jared Joselowitz explains how Ufonia evaluates and deploys Dora, a clinical voice agent, when conventional software safety practices such as A/B testing and rollback are not ethically available. He describes Matrix, a simulation framework that generates clinical conversations, judges hazards, and supports evidence-driven prompt optimization before carefully staged deployment to patients.

Table of Contents

  • Why clinical AI needs a different safety model
  • Dora and the hazards of conversational medicine
  • Matrix: simulating clinical conversations
  • Validating simulated patients and automated judges
  • Improving prompts with safety-weighted metrics
  • From simulation to staged deployment
  • Extending the safety case to voice and new modalities

Why clinical AI needs a different safety model

Jared Joselowitz is a research engineer at Ufonia, a UK healthcare company. Within its science team, he works on the safety and evaluation stack for Dora, a clinical conversational agent. The team’s job is to establish that the product is safe before a patient hears it.

Shipping AI to patients removes the normal safety nets of software delivery. Patients cannot be randomized into a worse variant: doing so is unethical and often illegal. A call cannot be undone once the agent has said something, and a model vendor’s benchmark result is not a defense in a post-incident review. The team therefore designs its work around those constraints.

Dora and the hazards of conversational medicine

Dora is a voice AI agent that phones patients for real clinical conversations, such as post-operative follow-ups and pre-operative checks. These are calls clinicians would normally make themselves. Dora is not intended to replace doctors; it takes a time-consuming task off their plate so they can focus elsewhere.

At the time of the talk, Dora had made around 200,000 real clinical calls across 20 UK hospitals, with a contract to reach one million patients over the following two years. The product had also launched in the United States, operating in two clinics with six more clinics signed across four states.

In a cataract-surgery example, Dora asks a patient whether their blurred vision affects distance or close-up vision, when it started, and whether they may resume swimming. It explains that blurry vision should improve rapidly in the first few days after surgery and advises avoiding swimming for a month to support healing. Because Dora asks about symptoms, gives advice, and answers questions, it is a regulated medical device.

Regulation reduces to three questions: what the software does, what could go wrong, and how the system ensures that it does not. For a conversational model interacting with patients, the possible failures are broad. Dora might miss a red-flag symptom such as sudden vision loss or severe pain; it might hallucinate an answer to a medical question; or it might ignore a distressed patient and continue without acknowledging that distress.

The normal software playbook is to release to a small percentage of users, watch dashboards, roll back when something breaks, and iterate. That playbook assumes the organization can afford to be wrong once. With patients, a small percentage can still mean hundreds or thousands of people receiving unproven care. A rollback cannot undo a completed call, and a dashboard turning red may mean a patient has already been harmed.

Matrix: simulating clinical conversations

The team looked to high-reliability industries such as self-driving cars, which simulate millions of miles before carrying passengers. For clinical history-taking, Ufonia built a simulation framework called Matrix. The premise is that simulation is the only ethical way to exercise hazards before exposing real people to them.

Matrix recreates a clinical conversation without involving a real patient. An LLM called PatBot plays a simulated patient. Hiring actors would not scale when the team needs to iterate quickly, run many scenarios in parallel, and update the underlying system. PatBot is conditioned on the precise scenario being tested, which specifies what the patient should try to do in the conversation, such as asking whether the agent is human or AI.

PatBot then speaks with Dora, the target system, to generate simulated dialogue. The scenarios are grounded in real clinical workflows rather than abstract situations. That grounding is central to making the simulation useful.

Validating simulated patients and automated judges

The team first checked script adherence: when PatBot was instructed to do something, did it do it? This filtered out weaker models that did not follow instructions, but adherence alone does not make a realistic patient. Real people vary: some speak verbosely with many hesitations, while others are direct and rely on short answers. The goal is to simulate a diverse range of personas rather than a single supposedly realistic patient.

Ufonia also ran a patient and public involvement study. Real patients were shown pairs of conversations: one between a real doctor and patient, and another between Dora and PatBot in Matrix. They were asked to identify the real patient. Across four conversations, the majority in three cases judged the simulated patient to be more realistic. This did not establish one universal kind of realism, but it showed that PatBot was realistic enough for the intended simulation.

Thousands of simulated conversations cannot be read manually, and the engineers are not clinicians. The team therefore uses another LLM as a judge, called BevJudge. It receives a simulated dialogue, expected behaviors, and clinician-defined hazardous scenarios, then returns a pass or fail along with the reason. This produces structured information about which hazards were triggered and what went wrong.

To validate BevJudge, the team created a corpus of 240 examples with ground truth about whether a hazard existed. Ten clinicians from ten specialties labeled the examples, and the judge was evaluated against them. The reported results placed the judge at least on par with, and slightly ahead of, the expert clinicians. Gemini 2.5 Pro, the leading model when the paper was written, achieved an F1 score of 0.96 and nearly perfect sensitivity. In healthcare, high sensitivity matters because it is preferable to overcall a potential hazard than to miss one.

Improving prompts with safety-weighted metrics

An automated judge makes large-scale grading possible, but a collection of pass and fail results does not by itself improve Dora. Earlier, the team would manually examine failing agents or prompts and perform prompt engineering. That approach is brittle, subjective, difficult to reproduce, and time-consuming. Formatting changes alone can swing benchmark performance by 76 percentage points, and reordering few-shot examples can move a model from near-random performance to near state of the art on some benchmarks.

The team instead uses prompt optimizers, particularly GEPA, which stands for genetic Pareto and comes from the creators of DSPy. The process starts with a definition of what good performance means. Data is passed through GEPA to identify failures; a strong LLM reflects on those failures and updates the prompt; and the process repeats. GEPA maintains a Pareto frontier of the best prompts until the available budget is exhausted.

This turns an hours- or days-long manual process into one that can often produce an optimized prompt in roughly 30 minutes to an hour. It is reproducible and leaves a clear audit trail and feedback loop. The work becomes a data-science problem: improving data, feature engineering, and the metric defined together with clinicians.

The metric cannot be a flat average accuracy score. It should be a cost matrix reflecting clinical consequences. If a red flag is present and correctly caught, that is good; missing it can be catastrophic. If no red flag exists but the system overcalls one, the patient may answer extra questions, which is inconvenient but not comparable to catastrophic harm. The system can therefore reward detection of red flags more strongly and penalize misses more heavily. Different clinical priorities can be supported by recompiling the prompt against a different metric.

The replacement for the reactive release loop is a flywheel: use real calls and data, add synthetic edge cases that may not arise naturally—such as rare symptoms or mistranscriptions—optimize the prompt, and run it through Matrix as a simulation safety gate. If something fails, the team can revisit the data, labels, or amount of data before proceeding to a gated deployment. Every deployment and new call adds data that can improve the system.

From simulation to staged deployment

Even realistic simulated patients are not real patients. Passing every simulation does not prove that Dora helps someone in practice; real-life situations can arise that are absent from simulation. Simulation is necessary but not sufficient. It is the fast inner loop that allows thousands of runs before anyone is exposed, while real patients are the outer loop where the actual proof comes from.

The transition happens in stages, with each stage earning the right to proceed to the next. After satisfactory simulation results, the team may conduct user testing, then supervised clinical evaluation with clinicians involved at every step. Voice actors can be used, but real patients are the most realistic source of evidence. Deployments remain monitored, and the autonomy granted to the system depends on the accumulated evidence.

Underneath this process, every call, dataset, pinned prompt, and judge verdict traces back to the specific hazard it addresses. That traceability is the real deliverable for regulation: the organization does not simply ship a model, but ships the evidence.

Extending the safety case to voice and new modalities

For teams building healthcare or other high-stakes systems, Joselowitz recommends defining exactly what harm means for the product, deliberately creating rare but dangerous cases instead of waiting for them to happen, using the evaluation metric as the real cost function, and pinning prompt versions while preserving traces.

The work is never complete. New modalities and languages create new hazards, but the same Matrix and prompt-optimization framework can be extended. Voice, for example, introduces backchanneling and interruptions. An agent may be midway through essential safety advice, such as instructing a patient to avoid bright lights, when the patient interrupts with an out-of-scope question. A weak model may forget the unfinished safety advice and answer the next question instead.

Matrix captures these failure modes. The system is still treated as a black box: the team identifies the new hazards, simulates them, and judges the results as it did for text. Voice is a new module within the same safety case, not a reason to begin the safety process from scratch. The central approach remains the same: simulate before the system reaches a patient, then use an optimization loop to improve it.
aiSummary: Ufonia 研究员 Jared Joselowitz 介绍临床语音智能体 Dora 如何借助模拟、聚焦风险的 LLM 裁判和以安全为权重的提示词优化，在接触患者前积累可靠证据。
oneSentenceSummary: Ufonia 研究员 Jared Joselowitz 介绍临床语音智能体 Dora 如何借助模拟、聚焦风险的 LLM 裁判和以安全为权重的提示词优化，在接触患者前积累可靠证据。
summary: 这场演讲指出，临床 AI 不能沿用传统软件的安全保障方式：一次不安全的对话在回滚之前就可能伤害患者。Joselowitz 介绍了 Ufonia 的模拟框架 Matrix：PatBot 扮演特定场景中的患者，BevJudge 则依据临床医生定义的风险来评估对话。他解释了团队如何验证模拟患者与裁判的可靠性，并使用 GEPA 按非对称成本矩阵优化提示词——漏掉危险信号的代价远高于不必要的升级处理。模拟是不可或缺的内部循环，之后还需经历用户测试、受监督的临床评估和持续监控的部署；每个提示词和判定结果都可以追溯到相应风险。这提供了一套在受监管、高风险环境中部署对话式 AI 的具体安全论证方法。

mainPoints.point: 临床 AI 需要在接触患者前建立证据，而非事后回滚
mainPoints.explanation: 演讲说明，对患者通话而言，随机投放有害变体或在事故后回滚都不符合伦理；发布决策的核心因此从快速迭代转为在部署前获得安全证据。

mainPoints.point: Matrix 将临床风险转化为可扩展的模拟对话
mainPoints.explanation: PatBot 根据有事实依据的临床场景与 Dora 交谈，而医生定义的预期行为和风险使这些模拟可被检验，不再只是泛泛的角色扮演。

mainPoints.point: 自动化裁判必须以临床事实基准验证
mainPoints.explanation: BevJudge 会判断是否通过并说明风险原因，但团队先将其与一套由临床医生标注的 240 个案例对照，尤其优先保障对危险漏诊症状的敏感性。

mainPoints.point: 以安全为权重的优化取代主观的提示词微调
mainPoints.explanation: GEPA 依据失败证据迭代提示词，并采用成本矩阵：漏掉危险信号的权重远高于造成不便的误报升级，同时保留可复现的审计轨迹。

mainPoints.point: 模拟不可或缺，但只是安全闭环的内部环节
mainPoints.explanation: 通过模拟并不能证明临床获益，因此该框架还要经过分阶段测试和受监控部署，并把通话、提示词、数据集与判定结果关联到具体风险。

keyQuotes: 其前提是，在让真实的人暴露于风险之前，模拟是唯一符合伦理的风险演练方式。
衡量指标不能是简单的平均准确率，而应是反映临床后果的成本矩阵。
模拟不可或缺，但并不充分。
组织交付的不是一个模型，而是支撑它的证据。
